title: Characterization of the dissemination of canine cancer misinformation on YouTube
screen_reason: The abstract reports a quantitative share of a defined video sample graded for misinformation: '61% of videos contained little to no misinformation' out of 99 unique videos. That is a CONTENT classification with a denominator, although it is stated in the inverse direction (the misinformation-carrying share, ~39%, is a complement I am not allowed to compute under R8). The DISCERN and PEMAT results are quality scores and are recorded as a QUALITY row, excluded from prevalence.

estimates.measure_type: % of canine-cancer YouTube videos graded as containing little to no misinformation (INVERSE polarity: the misinformation-carrying share is the unstated complement)
estimates.value_raw: 61% of videos contained little to no misinformation (sample of 99 unique videos)
estimates.denominator: 99 unique YouTube videos on canine cancer topics
estimates.definition: video graded into a 'little to no misinformation' category on a misinformation-level rating; the rating scale, rater qualifications and reference standard are not described in the abstract
estimates.source_quote: This study described the characteristics of 99 unique videos and used the validated DISCERN quality criteria for consumer health information and the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT) to characterize their usefulness. The overall median DISCERN quality score was 3 (out of 5), the median PEMAT understandability score was 72%, and 61% of videos contained little to no misinformation.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Not described in the abstract. No rater count, rubric, reference standard or reliability statistic is recoverable from the available text; researcher_coding is the presumptive code for a veterinary-journal video appraisal and should be re-checked against the full text.
estimates.moderator_quote: This study described the characteristics of 99 unique videos and used the validated DISCERN quality criteria for consumer health information and the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT) to characterize their usefulness.
estimates.notes: ABSTRACT ONLY, and several judgement calls follow from that. (1) POLARITY: the value is the share with little to NO misinformation. The prevalence-relevant figure is its complement (about 39% with some misinformation), which R8 forbids me from computing, so the row carries the stated 61% and the measure_type says so. An adjudicator merging this into a prevalence table must flip it deliberately. (2) The misinformation grading is separate from DISCERN/PEMAT and is a veracity judgement, so it is CONTENT, not QUALITY; but with no rubric in the abstract I cannot rule out that 'misinformation level' was an ordinal quality-style rating, hence borderline = true. (3) breadth = misleading is inferred from the graded wording ('little to no'), not stated. (4) denom_selection left blank because the abstract does not say whether the 99 videos came from a rank-truncated search; if the full text shows a top-N or first-pages search it should become curated. (5) year is blank: the abstract gives neither a data-collection date nor a publication year, and I will not guess one.

estimates.measure_type: median DISCERN quality score of canine-cancer YouTube videos (1-5 scale)
estimates.value_raw: The overall median DISCERN quality score was 3 (out of 5)
estimates.denominator: 99 unique YouTube videos on canine cancer topics
estimates.definition: DISCERN instrument for consumer health information, scored 1-5; median across videos
estimates.source_quote: The overall median DISCERN quality score was 3 (out of 5), the median PEMAT understandability score was 72%, and 61% of videos contained little to no misinformation.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: DISCERN applied by the study authors; number of raters and reliability not stated in the abstract.
estimates.moderator_quote: used the validated DISCERN quality criteria for consumer health information and the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT) to characterize their usefulness
estimates.notes: QUALITY row, excluded from prevalence per section 3. value_pct is a 1-5 scale point, NOT a percentage; value_kind = scale_score marks that. The median PEMAT understandability score of 72% is a second quality score on the same sample and is not recorded as a separate row because it measures understandability, not accuracy.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) '53% of videos were created by veterinarians' is a source-attribution share, not a misinformation share, so no row. (2) 'Videos with little to no misinformation had statistically significant higher DISCERN quality scores (3 vs. 2, p = .0001)' is a subgroup comparison of quality scores, not a prevalence estimate. (3) 'These data reveal similar rates of misinformation in videos on canine cancer compared to that reported for various human cancer topics' cites rates from elsewhere; R8 bars figures a paper cites from other work. (4) The misinformation-carrying share is not stated anywhere in the available text; only its complement is. (5) Everything about the sampling frame, coding rubric, rater training and reliability is unavailable, so all moderator codes on both rows are provisional and should be re-checked if the full text is obtained.

rob.design: Cannot be appraised: only the abstract is available. It reports 99 unique canine-cancer YouTube videos characterised with DISCERN and PEMAT plus an unspecified misinformation grading, with group comparisons by creator type (veterinarian vs client) and by misinformation level. No search strategy, date range, country, inclusion criteria, number of raters or intercoder reliability is given.
